title: Payload encoding benchmark: compact-binary vs JSON (lab notes)
body:
Purpose:
This is a working lab notebook for a small benchmark comparing payload encoding/serialization formats (JSON, Protobuf, CBOR, and a compact-binary custom wrapper we call CB-W) and their impact on observed end-to-end latency percentiles and estimated token-related cost per 1k requests under our hosted runtime. Goal is to decide whether switching to a compact encoding for high-throughput streaming clients is worth the engineering lift and backward compatibility tradeoffs.

Summary of findings (short):
- Compact-binary (CB-W) reduced median request size by ~45% vs raw JSON, yielding 12–18% p95 improvement in multi-turn streaming scenarios at moderate concurrency (8–32).
- Protobuf/CBOR sit between JSON and CB-W for size & latency. Protobuf performed best when payloads are highly structured; CBOR gave similar size to Protobuf but slightly higher CPU decode overhead for our node client.
- Network-bound scenarios (edge region clients, 50–100ms RTT) see larger gains in p95/p99 than colocated clients.
- Estimated dollars per 1k requests improved 6–9% for CB-W due to reduced egress and slight throughput gains in the serving runtime when fewer bytes are parsed per request.

Environment & runtime baseline:
- Model: open-13B-v0 (float16, KV cache warm), typical token output per request 120–320 tokens.
- Serving runtime: redwood-runtime v3.8.1 (linux, kernel 5.15), node shard pooling enabled, batching disabled (streaming mode).
- Hardware: Dedicated A100 (80GB) instances; client and server in same region for local runs; separate edge-run with 80ms added RTT.
- Client: TypeScript SDK (node 20), baseline JSON streaming implementation; alternate clients compiled with protobuf-js and a small C++ decoder for CB-W.
- Workload shapes: A=short-turn (120 tok output, 1-2 user tokens), B=multi-turn (avg 260 output, 4 user tokens), C=chat-burst (random 1–8 turns in session).
- Concurrency sweep: 1, 8, 16, 32 concurrent active sessions.

Payload formats tested (encoding & cost notes):
- JSON: plain text, streaming newline-delimited chunks (baseline).
- Protobuf: schema with optional tool-call fields; binary, length-prefixed frames.
- CBOR: generic binary map encoding, used as drop-in for structured messages.
- CB-W (compact-binary wrapper): custom compact token/field packing that collapses repetitive meta fields (session_id, role, chunk_index) into a compact header; designed for streaming where repeated header bytes are frequent.

Representative request sizes (avg bytes per request body, before transport compression):
- JSON: 8.2 KB
- Protobuf: 5.1 KB
- CBOR: 5.4 KB
- CB-W: 4.5 KB
(Note: gzip/deflate on transport reduces these by ~30–45% depending on format; CB-W compresses less efficiently than JSON due to entropy of packed fields; numbers above are raw sizes used for isolated bytes-transferred comparisons.)

Measurement method:
- Each experiment is 15 minutes with a 3-minute warm-up. We run 3 independent trials and report median of medians. Metrics collected: p50, p95, p99 end-to-end latency (ms), server CPU p95, bytes transmitted per request, observed retransmissions (none significant), and downstream cost estimate (approx dollars per 1k requests).
- Cost model assumptions: API egress weighted at $0.00012 per MB (internal equivalence), compute amortized as $0.00008 per second of GPU time per request (very rough internal back-of-envelope). We treat lower bytes => lower egress cost and slightly lower token processing overhead if fewer parse-related op cycles are used.

Results (selected slice): concurrency=16, workload=B (multi-turn), regional RTT=25ms (colocated)

ASCII table: format | p50(ms) | p95(ms) | p99(ms) | bytes/request | est $/1k
- JSON    | 210     | 420     | 780    | 8.2KB         | $0.52
- Protobuf| 190     | 380     | 720    | 5.1KB         | $0.48
- CBOR    | 195     | 390     | 740    | 5.4KB         | $0.49
- CB-W   | 180     | 345     | 660    | 4.5KB         | $0.47

Notes on table: p95 improvements are relative to JSON baseline; p99 gains are smaller in absolute ms but meaningful for SLOs. Dollar estimates fold egress + a tiny compute delta (not full infra pricing).

Edge-run (simulated RTT add 80ms, concurrency=16):
- JSON p95: 550ms, CB-W p95: 460ms, approx 16% improvement. Edge cases show larger win because network transmission time scales with payload size more directly.

CPU/parse overhead observation (server side):
- JSON parsing for streaming incremental chunks costs CPU spikes when chunk boundaries are small. Protobuf/CBOR decoder in C++ had slightly lower p95 CPU usage. CB-W decoder was lightweight (C++ micro-decoder) and avoided repeated map allocations -> lower p95 server CPU by ~8%.

Bandwidth vs compression tradeoffs:
- Because JSON compresses well (repeated whitespace/keys), gzip reduced JSON payloads relatively more than CB-W, narrowing the raw bytes advantage. In our runs we disabled transport-level compression for a subset of tests (simulating TLS passthrough/edge proxies that avoid recompression). When compression is allowed, byte differences shrink and latency gains move from bytes to CPU/parse efficiencies.

Developer ergonomics & compatibility:
- JSON: highest developer ergonomics; immediate backwards-compatible; easiest to debug with logs.
- Protobuf: requires schema cadence; good for structured outputs and typed SDKs.
- CBOR: easy to adopt via existing libs; less human-readable but schema-free.
- CB-W: smallest wire size for our use-case but requires bespoke encoder/decoder and versioning scheme; more risk in partial rollouts.

Risk and rollout considerations:
- Rolling CB-W to public SDKs needs feature detection and staged rollout (canary clients + server-side header to indicate accepted encodings).
- Backwards compatibility: ensure server accepts JSON and CB-W simultaneously for 6+ months.
- Observability: binary encodings require additional instrumentation points to expose token counts for billing and QA; need to add a lightweight header/sidecar that emits parsed token counts to tracing pipeline.

Conclusions / recommended next steps (short list):
1) Do a 2-week prototyping spike to integrate Protobuf and CB-W decoders into the TypeScript SDK (PR exists) and add byte-level telemetry to the console. Goal: surface real-world traffic delta when a small fraction of clients opt-in.
2) For immediate wins, add server-side optional support for Protobuf: low lift, good ergonomics for typed clients.
3) Reserve CB-W for high-volume customers behind a feature flag (enterprise-only early access). CB-W rollout strategy: private beta -> canary -> enterprise opt-in.
4) Run a production shadow test with 5% of traffic encoded as Protobuf and CB-W for 48 hours (measure p95, p99, and billing parity).

Open questions / TODOs:
- Quantify the impact of payload compression enabled by edge proxies in production (some CDNs recompress). Need to run CDN-aware runs.
- Cost model refinement: replace crude egress estimate with actual cloud egress pricing per-region and account for per-request metadata egress.
- Add more sessionized workloads (long conversations with many small turns) to better stress parsing overhead.

Appendix: short sample payloads (trimmed)
- JSON example: {
  "session_id": "s-1234", "role": "assistant", "chunk": "...text..."
}
- Protobuf snippet: length-prefixed frame with fields: session_id (str), role (enum), chunk (bytes)
- CB-W conceptual header: [h: one-byte flags][sid: 8 bytes][idx: 1 byte] + packed chunk bytes (no repeated key bytes)

Lab contact: Elena Rivers (elena@redwood.com) — reach out for repro scripts and the small C++ decoder binary.

End of notebook.
